findings.description: Static date regex `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` is flagged as a potential ReDoS pattern, but it has no nested/ambiguous quantifiers and cannot backtrack catastrophically
findings.reasoning: The pattern consists of three fixed-width, non-overlapping `\d{n}` groups separated by literal dashes, anchored with `^` and `$`. Each quantifier has an exact repetition count (`{4}`, `{2}`, `{2}`) and the alternatives cannot match the same substring, so the matching engine performs essentially one comparison per input position — O(n) worst case. There is no nested quantifier (`(a+)+`), no overlapping alternation, and no unbounded repetition over a group. Additionally it is a module-level compiled literal (`re.ASCII` set), so no user input can influence the pattern. The query is a "regex usage listing" informational rule, not evidence of ReDoS.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Pattern is a module-level constant string literal; only the subject `instance` is user-controlled, which cannot affect regex complexity.
evidence.notes: Rule py/regex-usage-listing is a listing/inventory rule; no untrusted pattern input and no exponential backtracking structure.

findings.description: Regex `^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9_]*$` used for JSON-path compatible property names is a linear-time character-class pattern, not a ReDoS vector
findings.reasoning: Single leading character class followed by one repeated character class (`[...]*`), wrapped in anchors. The repetition applies to a single character class that cannot overlap itself ambiguously and there is no alternation or nested group, so the engine makes a deterministic linear pass. Only the matched subject comes from user data; the pattern is a compiled module-level constant. No catastrophic backtracking is possible.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Constant pattern literal; subject from property names only affects input length, giving O(n) matching.
evidence.notes: Classic linear pattern; informational listing rule, no vulnerability.

findings.description: `re.search(r"\d+", key)` in a repository maintenance/build script is a trivial single-quantifier pattern with no ReDoS potential and no production attack surface
findings.reasoning: Two independent reasons this is a false positive: (1) The pattern `\d+` is a single unbounded quantifier over a single character class with no nesting or alternation — worst case linear scan, no backtracking amplification. (2) The file is a developer maintenance script under `json/bin/` that walks the test suite directory (`TESTS.iterdir()`, `version.rglob("*.json")`) to annotate specification links; it is not imported by the library, is not installed as runtime code, and its inputs are repo-controlled test-suite keys. There is no attacker-controlled input path.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: key originates from repository test-suite JSON keys enumerated by the script itself; no network/CLI untrusted input, and the regex is a literal.
evidence.notes: Build/dev tooling + trivial regex => not exploitable.

findings.description: `open(path)` in the deprecated jsonschema CLI opens the file path supplied by the local operator on the command line — intended functionality, no privilege boundary is crossed
findings.reasoning: `_Outputter.load(path)` is invoked from `main()` with paths taken from the CLI's own positional arguments (`instance_files`), i.e. the value is chosen by the user running the `jsonschema` command. The CLI is explicitly deprecated (module-level DeprecationWarning) and its entire purpose is to read the JSON files the operator names. A local user who can pass argv already has filesystem read access as themselves, so there is no traversal/arbitrary-file-read escalation. There is no code path where a remote/untrusted party supplies this `path` (it is not derived from JSON content or from schema references).

evidence.dataflow_analysis: path <- argparse positional/`--instance` argument provided by the local caller of the CLI. No remote- or content-derived source reaches open().
evidence.notes: Rule custom/py/file-open-listing is a listing rule; the sink is the documented CLI behaviour.

findings.description: The "regex" format checker compiles an instance-supplied string as a regular expression (re.compile(instance)), so attacker-controlled data reaching the `format: regex` checker controls regex compilation
findings.reasoning: This is the only location where the *instance* being validated (rather than the schema) supplies the regular expression. `re.compile()` does not perform backtracking matching, so classic catastrophic-backtracking ReDoS is not directly reachable here; however, compiling attacker-supplied patterns does consume CPU/memory proportional to pattern complexity and can raise RecursionError/MemoryError on pathological inputs. Exploitation requires the application to (a) validate untrusted data and (b) opt into format checking with the default FormatChecker (or a checker including "regex"). This is intended behaviour of a format checker named "regex", therefore it is not a clear vulnerability of the library but a resource-consumption consideration for downstream users — warrants manual review rather than a confirmed tp/fp.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: instance (validated JSON value, fully attacker-controlled when validating untrusted payloads) -> re.compile(instance) at jsonschema/_format.py:419. Reached via FormatChecker.check() when a schema declares {"format": "regex"} and the caller passes format_checker=FormatChecker().
evidence.notes: No fullmatch/search is performed on the compiled pattern in this function, so catastrophic backtracking is not triggered here; impact is limited to compile-time resource usage. Library considers this the documented purpose of the format.

findings.description: patternProperties keyword applies schema-declared regexes to instance property names via re.search — schema patterns are trusted configuration, not attacker input
findings.reasoning: The dynamic regex here (`pattern`) comes from the JSON Schema itself (`schema["patternProperties"]`), which is configuration supplied by the application developer — the same trust level as application code. The attacker-controlled value (`k`, the property name of the instance) is the *matched subject*, not the pattern. ReDoS would require the schema author to deliberately write a vulnerable pattern; the library cannot and does not attempt to police user-provided patterns. This is the documented semantics of JSON Schema `patternProperties`, so the CodeQL "dynamic regex" result is a false positive for a library-level vulnerability.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Source: schema["patternProperties"] keys (trusted validation schema). Sink: re.search(pattern, k) at jsonschema/_keywords.py:22. The tainted-for-security value (instance property name k) is the haystack, not the regex.
evidence.notes: Same pattern repeats at _keywords.py:218, _legacy_keywords.py:383, _utils.py:82 and _utils.py:317; all operate on schema-provided patterns.

findings.description: Schema-supplied regular expressions from the `pattern` keyword are executed with `re.search` against untrusted instance data, allowing ReDoS (catastrophic backtracking) or regex-injection style DoS when the JSON Schema is not fully trusted.
findings.reasoning:
`pattern` is a direct pass-through of the schema's regex into `re.search(patrn, instance)` with no complexity limit, no timeout wrapper and no validation of the pattern itself (unlike the `regex` format checker which at least compiles it). Two distinct trust directions are risky here:

1. Untrusted schema + attacker-controlled instance string: a malicious schema author supplies a catastrophic pattern such as `(a+)+$` and the instance string `"a"*50000 + "!"`, causing exponential backtracking and pinning a CPU core (Python's `re` has no timeout).
2. Trusted schema, untrusted data: even a "reasonable" schema pattern can be paired with pathological input to cause super-linear blowup (nested quantifiers/alternation).

Because jsonschema is commonly used to validate data from remote/untrusted sources against schemas that may themselves be fetched from remote registries, this is a plausible availability issue, but exploitation depends entirely on the deployment's trust model — hence manual review rather than a confirmed true positive.

evidence.code_context: jsonschema/_keywords.py:216-224 -> pattern(validator, patrn, instance, schema) calls re.search(patrn, instance); patrn comes straight from the schema's "pattern" keyword, instance is the user-supplied JSON value. Registered for all drafts in validators.py ("pattern": _keywords.pattern).
evidence.dataflow_analysis: source: schema dict value schema['pattern'] -> validator function argument patrn -> sink: re.search(patrn, instance). No `re.escape`, no pattern whitelist, no timeout/threading guard anywhere in the call chain.
evidence.notes: Query 2/4/5 all point at this same sink (line 218 in raw pattern-dump, 22 in others is the sibling patternProperties function). Python `re` cannot be interrupted; a 30-char catastrophic pattern over a 50 KB string can hang for minutes.

findings.description: `patternProperties` executes each schema-supplied regex against every instance property name via `re.search`, with no timeout or complexity guard — ReDoS when schemas are untrusted.
findings.reasoning: This is the nested-loop variant of the `pattern` sink: for each attacker-controlled property name `k` in the instance, every pattern from `schema['patternProperties']` is compiled and run via `re.search`. The multiplicative factor makes DoS cheaper for the attacker — one catastrophic pattern is evaluated N times, once per property key, and `re.search` matches against the whole key string. There is no `re.escape`, no length cap on keys and no regex timeout. Exploitation again hinges on whether the schema is attacker-influenced; if the schema is fully trusted the risk reduces to pathological-input DoS only, so this needs manual trust-model review.

evidence.code_context: jsonschema/_keywords.py:16-25: for pattern, subschema in patternProperties.items(): for k, v in instance.items(): if re.search(pattern, k). Registered for every draft in validators.py:624,662,705,750,797,845.
evidence.dataflow_analysis: schema['patternProperties'] keys -> `pattern` -> re.search(pattern, k) where k is an instance key (attacker data). Amplification: patterns x keys.
evidence.notes: Same underlying sink as _utils.py:82 and _legacy_keywords.py:383; CodeQL flags this location in queries 2, 4 and 5.

findings.description: All `patternProperties` patterns are concatenated with `|` into a single alternation regex and then executed via `re.search` against each instance property — the concatenation amplifies catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS).
findings.reasoning: `find_additional_properties` builds a single regex by joining every `patternProperties` key with `|` and then runs it against each instance property name inside a loop over the whole instance. Joining patterns with alternation is a well-known ReDoS amplifier: independent catastrophic sub-patterns interact, and a schema author (or anyone who can influence the schema) only needs one bad branch — e.g. patterns `(a+)+` and `(a|a)*b` become `(a+)+|(a|a)*b`, which backtracks exponentially on a long `aaaa...` key. Because the joined pattern is also unescaped and unvalidated, this is the highest-signal ReDoS location in the package. Manual review because exploitability depends on the schema trust model.

evidence.code_context: jsonschema/_utils.py:71-86. `patterns = "|".join(schema.get("patternProperties", {}))` then `re.search(patterns, property)` per instance key. Called from _keywords.additionalProperties and find_additional_properties-based validators (additionalProperties: false path).
evidence.dataflow_analysis: schema['patternProperties'] keys --"|".join--> patterns -> re.search(patterns, property) for each attacker-controlled property name. Nested loop + alternation concatenation = amplification of backtracking complexity.
evidence.notes: CodeQL queries 2 and 4 both flag line 82; query 5 pattern-dump reports the `patterns` variable here.

findings.description: Legacy `find_evaluated_property_keys_by_schema` executes schema-supplied `patternProperties` regexes via `re.search` on instance keys without any regex guard (unevaluatedProperties path).
findings.reasoning: Same unchecked `re.search(pattern, instance_property)` sink as `_keywords.patternProperties`, here in the legacy evaluator used for `unevaluatedProperties`/`unevaluatedItems` resolution across subschemas (allOf/anyOf/oneOf/dependentSchemas recursion means each pattern can be evaluated many times). A catastrophic pattern in an untrusted schema plus a long key triggers exponential backtracking; conversely long adversarial keys against a super-linear schema pattern cause CPU exhaustion. Depends on the schema trust model → manual review.

evidence.code_context: jsonschema/_legacy_keywords.py:378-388 inside find_evaluated_property_keys_by_schema; loops instance keys x patternProperties patterns -> re.search. Recursively invoked from the allOf/oneOf/anyOf and dependentSchemas blocks below (lines ~390-420).
evidence.dataflow_analysis: schema['patternProperties'] -> pattern -> re.search(pattern, property); property from instance. Multiplied by subschema recursion.
evidence.notes: Flagged by CodeQL queries 2, 4 and 5 at line 383.

findings.description: `find_evaluated_property_keys_by_schema` (non-legacy) executes schema `patternProperties` regexes with `re.search` over instance property names, allowing ReDoS during unevaluatedProperties evaluation.
findings.reasoning: Duplicate of the `_legacy_keywords.py:383` sink but in the current `_utils.find_evaluated_property_keys_by_schema` implementation that is used by 2019-09/2020-12 `unevaluatedProperties`. It is called recursively for each subschema in `allOf`/`oneOf`/`anyOf`/`dependentSchemas`, so a single catastrophic `patternProperties` pattern is executed (patterns × keys × subschemas) times. No timeout, no pattern validation, no length limit. Actual risk depends on whether the schema is trusted, so manual review.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: schema['patternProperties'] keys -> pattern -> re.search(pattern, property); property is attacker data. Recursion multiplies evaluation count.

findings.description: Static, non-backtracking regex `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` used via `_RE_DATE.fullmatch` — not a ReDoS candidate
findings.reasoning: Query 5 flagged `instance` at _format.py:432 as a regex-pattern dump entry, but `instance` is the *subject* of the match, not the pattern. The actual pattern is the module-level constant `_RE_DATE = re.compile(r"^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$", re.ASCII)` defined at line 18. This pattern contains only fixed-width character classes with no quantified alternation, nested quantifiers, or overlapping repetition, so catastrophic backtracking is impossible — matching is linear in the input length. Input is also type-gated (`isinstance(instance, str)`) and length-bounded in practice by the `{4}-{2}-{2}` anchors. This is a false positive.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: The tainted/dynamic element at line 432 is the match subject `instance`, not a regex pattern. Pattern is an immutable module-level constant; no attacker-controlled pattern compilation occurs.
evidence.notes: ReDoS requires nested/ambiguous quantifiers. `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` is deterministic and linear-time. Not exploitable.

findings.description: SSRF / arbitrary-scheme fetch: `_RefResolver.resolve_remote` fetches an attacker-controlled `$ref` URI with `requests.get(uri)` (or `urlopen(uri)` fallback) without any host/scheme allow-listing, so a schema containing a hostile `$ref` makes the application issue requests to internal services or read local files.
findings.code_snippet:
scheme = urlsplit(uri).scheme

        if scheme in self.handlers:
            result = self.handlers[scheme](uri)
        elif scheme in ["http", "https"] and requests:
            # Requests has support for detecting the correct encoding of
            # json over http
            result = requests.get(uri).json()
        else:
            # Otherwise, pass off to urllib and assume utf-8
            with urlopen(uri) as url:  # noqa: S310
                result = json.loads(url.read().decode("utf-8"))
findings.reasoning:
`uri` is fully attacker-influenced: it originates from a `$ref` value inside the JSON Schema being validated. The path is: `$ref` in schema -> `_RefResolver.resolve()` (line ~1104 `self._urljoin_cache(self.resolution_scope, ref)`) -> `_remote_cache(url)` -> `resolve_from_url()` -> `resolve_remote(url)` (line 1122) -> `requests.get(uri).json()` at line 1225 / `urlopen(uri)` at line 1228.

There is no allow-list of hosts, no blocking of private/link-local IP ranges, no scheme restriction beyond "if it's not http/https use urlopen", and no redirect handling. Consequences:
* `$ref: "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/"` -> cloud metadata SSRF (the JSON body is parsed and returned to the caller / included in error output).
* `$ref: "http://internal-service:8080/admin"` -> internal port scanning and blind/internal GET requests (result is also cached in `self.store[uri]`, so data retrieved is retained).
* `$ref: "file:///etc/passwd"` -> falls into the `else` branch and reads arbitrary local files through `urlopen`.
* `cache_remote` defaults to True (line 926), so responses are stored and reachable by later schema keywords.

The class is deprecated (v4.18.0) and the docstring warns about remote resolution, but the code is still shipped, exported as the `jsonschema.RefResolver` public alias (`__init__.py:39`, `validators.py:70`) and used by `jsonschema/cli.py:272`. Applications that validate untrusted schemas (e.g. API accepting a JSON Schema document, or schemas with user-supplied `$id`/`$ref`) are therefore exposed to SSRF/LFI. Note also that the deprecation warning is only emitted on the `referencing`-based path (`_warn_for_remote_retrieve`), not from `_RefResolver.resolve_remote`, so this path fetches silently.

No sanitization of scheme/host; only dispatch on scheme presence in self.handlers (empty by default).

findings.description: Default remote `$ref` retrieval in `_warn_for_remote_retrieve` performs `urlopen(Request(uri))` on a URI taken from the untrusted schema's `$ref`; the deprecation warning does not prevent the SSRF, and arbitrary schemes (file://, internal http hosts) are accepted.
findings.reasoning: This is the *default* retrieval hook installed on every validator via `_REMOTE_WARNING_REGISTRY = SPECIFICATIONS.combine(referencing.Registry(retrieve=_warn_for_remote_retrieve))` (line ~123). Whenever a validated schema contains an unresolvable `$ref`, `referencing` calls this function with the attacker-controlled URI, and the code performs a blocking `urlopen` to it *before* emitting the warning. There is no validation of host, IP range, port or scheme — `urllib` also accepts `file://`, `ftp://`, etc. The retrieved bytes are parsed as JSON and handed back to the referencing registry, so internal-service responses and local files are effectively read/exfiltrated into the validation result or surfaced in error messages. Because the warning happens after the request, it provides no mitigation (and DeprecationWarning is hidden by default).

    referencing.Registry(retrieve=_warn_for_remote_retrieve),

Every created validator class uses this combined registry, so any schema with an unresolvable external $ref triggers the fetch.
evidence.dataflow_analysis: schema['$ref'] (untrusted) -> referencing resolver -> Registry._retrieve(uri) -> _warn_for_remote_retrieve(uri) -> Request(uri) -> urlopen(request) -> json.load(response). No allow-listing/sanitization between source and sink.
evidence.notes: Authors acknowledge the risk in the warning text, but the fetch is still performed unconditionally; the mitigation available to callers is to pass a custom registry, which most do not.

findings.description: Unvalidated ``$ref`` URI passed straight to urllib's urlopen allows arbitrary scheme fetches (SSRF / local file disclosure)
findings.code_snippet:
else:
            # Otherwise, pass off to urllib and assume utf-8
            with urlopen(uri) as url:  # noqa: S310
                result = json.loads(url.read().decode("utf-8"))
findings.reasoning:
This is the second, distinct network-access sink inside `_RefResolver.resolve_remote`. Unlike the `requests.get` branch (which is restricted to the `http`/`https` schemes), this fallback branch executes for *any* scheme that is not registered in `self.handlers` and not http/https when `requests` is absent or when the scheme differs — e.g. `file://`, `ftp://`, `gopher://`, `data:` — because `urlopen` (imported at module level from `urllib.request`) happily supports arbitrary URL schemes including `file://`.

The `uri` argument originates directly from the schema being validated: `resolve()` → `_remote_cache(url)` → `resolve_from_url(url)` (line 1122 `document = self.resolve_remote(url)`) where `url` is `urljoin(resolution_scope, ref)` and `ref` comes from an attacker-supplied `$ref`/`$id`/`$schema` keyword in the JSON document. There is no allow-list, no scheme restriction, no private-IP/host filtering, and no `file://` block anywhere in this path, as confirmed by grepping for handlers/allow-lists (no os.path/ipaddress/allowlist validation in validators.py).

Impact: an application that validates untrusted JSON Schema using the (deprecated but still shipped and re-exported as `jsonschema.RefResolver`) `_RefResolver` will perform attacker-chosen requests, enabling SSRF against internal services/cloud metadata endpoints and — via `file://` — local file disclosure of any JSON-parseable file readable by the process (e.g. `{"$ref": "file:///etc/.../some.json"}` plus error-message disclosure patterns). The `# noqa: S310` comment shows the maintainers knowingly suppressed the lint warning rather than adding validation.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Attacker-controlled JSON schema contains `$ref`/`$id`/`$schema` with an arbitrary URI -> Validator resolution scope -> _RefResolver.resolve(ref) (line ~1100) builds url = urljoin(resolution_scope, ref) -> _remote_cache(url) -> resolve_from_url(url) -> line 1122 `document = self.resolve_remote(url)` -> line 1228 `urlopen(uri)` (no scheme/subnet validation). Grep for handlers/allow-lists shows no host/IP validation; only a user-supplied `handlers` dict can intercept schemes, otherwise raw urlopen.
evidence.notes: Sibling sink at line 1221 (requests.get) was submitted separately; this branch is materially different because it permits non-HTTP schemes such as file:// (local file read) and ftp/gopher. `# noqa: S310` / `# noqa: S310` shows lint suppression instead of validation. Base class is deprecated (v4.18.0) but still importable/used, and the modern `_warn_for_remote_retrieve` path has the same 'retrieve whatever the schema says' behavior.
